corrections.why_faster: Not stated by the suite; from the sources: Zig splits with std.mem.splitScalar and counts in a std.StringHashMap(u32) (flat open-addressing table) whose keys are borrowed slices into the original text, with the map allocated from an ArenaAllocator that is freed in one step, so no per-word allocation, copy or free happens. C++ extracts each word with std::istringstream operator>> (sentry and locale-aware whitespace skipping) into a std::string and inserts into a node-based std::unordered_map<std::string,int>, one heap node per distinct word, freed when the map is destroyed inside the timed run(); the C version strdup()s the whole text every iteration, tokenizes with strtok_r and strdup()s every new key into uthash. Since the generator makes nearly every one of the 50,000 words (3 to 8 random letters) distinct (inference from prepare()), the C/C++ side pays roughly one malloc and free per word per iteration. The win is the standard-library container and the zero-copy idiom, not code generation.
corrections.caveats: Standard-library and idiom comparison, not code generation: Zig keys a flat hash map with zero-copy slices into the text inside an arena, while the C++ test uses istringstream plus a node-based unordered_map with copied keys and the C test strdup()s the text and every key; a C++ version with std::string_view keys and a flat hash map would likely close most of the gap (inference, not measured). Both sides do the same split, count and max-scan over the same text and the suite checks the checksum. Zig's production row is ReleaseSafe built for the native CPU (b.standardTargetOptions default), while the prod C/C++ rows are generic x86-64 -O2 with hardening flags; the -O3 -march=native Fast and Unsafe rows and the PGO rows were also compared and still lose, and the Makefiles pass the LTO flags only at link time, so no C/C++ row had real LTO. The same test is catalogued for Java (lang:java/kostya/langarena#etc-words), where the same C++ weakness drives the result. LangArena's README calls it not an objective, peer-reviewed or industry-standard suite (rules and library choices are the author's judgment) and says AI tools helped translate the tests from Crystal, with the author reviewing them. Each configuration is timed once per monthly run (no repeats or variance within a run); every language, C and C++ included, runs 20% of the iterations as untimed warm-up and checksums are verified. The per-benchmark ratios are derived from the results files, not stated by the suite. Rows were picked by the search agent as text tests where a Rust, Zig or Go production row beats every C and C++ row; most other text tests in the suite go the other way (for example Base64::Encode and Base64::Decode, where C is about 3x faster than Rust, and Distance::Jaro, a tie).

notes: Confirm at A: every number matches the Etc::Words-runtime rows of the 2026-10-05 results file, and four earlier monthly runs give the same 1.71-1.72x lead. Shortcomings to record: a container and idiom win (zero-copy slice keys, flat StringHashMap and arena against istringstream plus node-based unordered_map with copied keys), Zig production row is ReleaseSafe for the native CPU against generic -O2 prod C/C++ (the -O3 -march=native rows also lose), one timing per configuration per run, subjective AI-assisted suite. Metadata checks out (MIT, 41 stars, 16 forks, not a fork, last commit 2026-10-08).

corrections.caveats: Direct port of Lemire's fast_float, which is already catalogued (https://github.com/fastfloat/fast_float, tier A); against that C++ original the Rust port is at parity or slower (C++ faster on all six AMD Rome datasets by 9-22%, derived from page data), so the win over strtod is the Eisel-Lemire algorithm, not the language. The algorithm was merged into Rust's core library (the repo description reads 'now part of Rust core'; RUSTSEC-2024-0379 cites rust-lang/rust PR 86761), so the README's 2-8x lead over FromStr is obsolete for current Rust. Security: RUSTSEC-2024-0379 (GHSA-x8jh-xj3x-gx3c, informational 'unsound': undefined behaviour when checking input length, fixed in the repo by issue #28 but never published, plus many safe functions with non-local safety requirements, and the crate is flagged unmaintained) and RUSTSEC-2025-0003 (GHSA-8655-xgh5-5vvq, memory exposure: fast_float::common::AsciiStr::first reads without a bounds check and segfaults on an empty input); neither has a patched release, and the advisories point to the fast-float2 fork. First-party benchmarks on Rust 1.49 with C/C++ compiler flags unstated; the strtod row is whatever libc each machine had (macOS libc on the Intel and M1 tables, presumably glibc on AMD Rome, not stated).

notes: Numbers match the README tables exactly; tier C stands (first-party, C/C++ flags unstated). Shortcomings to record: no language win, two RustSec advisories with no patched release (unsound length check, out-of-bounds read on empty input), unmaintained since 2021-07-03, algorithm now in Rust core so the from_str comparison is obsolete. corrections.workload: Scan a generated HTML template of 50,000 table rows (about 150,000 {{ key }} placeholders with surrounding spaces, plus single-brace decoys) byte by byte, trim each key, look it up in a 150,001-entry variable map and append the value to a pre-reserved output buffer; 50 timed iterations after 10 untimed warm-up iterations.
corrections.why_faster: Not stated by the suite; from the sources (inference, not profiled): the scanning loop is the same everywhere, but Go takes the key as text[i+2:j] and strings.TrimSpace, both zero-copy because Go strings are immutable slices, and looks it up in Go's built-in map (Swiss tables since Go 1.24). The C version mallocs, memcpy()s and frees every key (about 150,000 malloc/free pairs per iteration) to get a NUL-terminated string for uthash's HASH_FIND_STR (Jenkins hash, chained buckets, keys and values in separate strdup'd blocks, strlen on each value); C++ builds two std::string temporaries per key with substr and trim (heap-allocated for the 17-character ' FIRST_NAMEnnnnn ' slices) and looks them up in a node-based std::unordered_map<std::string,std::string>. Per-placeholder allocation of the C side alone is about the size of the 2.9 ms per-iteration gap (estimate). The win is the string model and map idiom, not code generation.
corrections.caveats: Small margin (1.10-1.18x over the best C/C++ row in five monthly runs) that rests on allocation and container idioms: the C test mallocs and frees a copy of every key, and the C++ test builds std::string temporaries, where C with a length-keyed HASH_FIND or C++ with std::string_view keys and a flat map would avoid that (inference, not measured); Go does not win on codegen, and its per-byte strings.Builder.WriteByte loop is if anything heavier than C's direct buffer store. Go's harness calls runtime.GC() after warm-up so the timed loop starts with a clean heap, but collections during the loop (a new output buffer of about 1.5x the template per iteration) are timed; Go uses 75 MB peak RSS against 41 MB for C. The C/C++ prod rows are -O2 with hardening flags, but the -O3 -march=native Fast and Unsafe rows and the PGO rows were also compared and lose, and the Makefiles pass the LTO flags only at link time. Go also loses badly on other text tests in the same suite (Etc::LogParser 30.9 s). LangArena's README calls it not an objective, peer-reviewed or industry-standard suite (rules and library choices are the author's judgment) and says AI tools helped translate the tests from Crystal, with the author reviewing them. Each configuration is timed once per monthly run (no repeats or variance within a run); every language, C and C++ included, runs 20% of the iterations as untimed warm-up and checksums are verified. The per-benchmark ratios are derived from the results files, not stated by the suite. Rows were picked by the search agent as text tests where a Rust, Zig or Go production row beats every C and C++ row; most other text tests in the suite go the other way (for example Base64::Encode and Base64::Decode, where C is about 3x faster than Rust, and Distance::Jaro, a tie).

notes: Confirm, upgraded C to A: the numbers match the Template::Parse-runtime rows of the 2026-10-05 results file, the same algorithm runs on every side, and four earlier monthly runs show the same 1.10-1.15x lead, so the record's noise concern is unfounded. Shortcomings to record: small margin driven by allocation idioms (malloc'd key copies in C, std::string temporaries in C++, zero-copy substrings and a Swiss-table map in Go), not codegen; 1.8x the memory of C; one timing per configuration per run; subjective AI-assisted suite.
